title: The Narrow Road to the Deep North: the Hut, the Barrier, and the Withered Field
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ueno, the birth in Iga
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unrecorded; defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: In a castle town of Iga ringed by mountains, a second son is born to a Matsuo household that holds samurai privilege without samurai income. They name him Kinsaku. The province's other export is ninjutsu, and biographers three centuries later, weighing the family name against the boy's later appetite for walking, will wonder aloud whether some of that training reached him. Nothing in the record says so. The record gives a landowning family with a sword's worth of status and a domain called Tōdō. The boy leaves both before he is thirty.
suggested_refs: The Matsuo family house at Ueno, present-day Iga, Mie Prefecture
sources: Donald Keene, The Narrow Road to Oku, introduction

stops.name: Ueno, service to Tōdō Yoshitada
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the accounts differ on his role and on the exact year of entry
stops.campa: In his late teens Kinsaku enters the household of Tōdō Yoshitada, a young kinsman of the ruling house, as page or as kitchen servant; the accounts differ. Master and servant share one appetite, haikai no renga, the comic linked verse then fashionable in samurai halls and merchant back rooms alike. They study under a Kyoto teacher. The boy takes the pen name Sōbō and publishes his first surviving poem in 1662. Rank divides the two of them; a form of verse that needs two people to finish a single thought does not.
suggested_refs: The 1665 hyakuin, a hundred-verse renku composed with Yoshitada and their circle

stops.name: Ueno, the death of Yoshitada
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unrecorded; defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Yoshitada dies suddenly, still young, and the household that gave Kinsaku a footing dissolves under him. He considers taking vows. Instead he drifts loose from Ueno toward Kyoto, no longer bound to samurai service and not yet bound to anything else. Late in life he will recall the years around this break in two sentences no scholar can date or verify: that he once coveted an official post with a tenure of land, and that there was a time when he was fascinated with the ways of homosexual love. He does not say which he gave up first.
stops.quote: the alternatives battled in my mind and made my life restless
stops.quote_source: Bashō recalling his uncertainty over becoming a full-time poet; quoted in Wikipedia, 'Matsuo Bashō' (underlying work and translator not named there)
suggested_refs: The vague autobiographical passage on his youth, whose factual status Wikipedia itself declines to settle

stops.name: Edo, arrival in the shogun's city
stops.date_confidence: attested to spring 1672; day unrecorded
stops.campa: He publishes Kai Ōi, The Seashell Game, and in spring moves to the shogun's city to make his name in its growing haikai world. He clerks a while for the waterworks and lodges near the merchant district of Nihonbashi. Within two years the profession's inner circle admits him and Kitamura Kigin passes him its secret teachings; by 1675 he signs himself Tōsei, and by 1680 twenty disciples print a book of their own verse under his name. Roland Barthes will come to this city to read the haiku as a sign refusing to mean, and Ian Fleming will tour its baths for a novel.
suggested_refs: Kai Ōi (The Seashell Game), 1672
The Best Poems of Tōsei's Twenty Disciples, 1680

stops.name: Fukagawa, the plant that gives the name
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: A disciple gives him a cottage across the Sumida in Fukagawa, then an unfashionable edge of the city, and plants a bashō by the door, a Japanese banana whose broad leaves shred in the first hard wind. He takes the plant's name for his own. He is withdrawing from an establishment that has just crowned him: twenty students, a school, a market position in a trade where masters were paid to judge verse. Tradition adds that he studies Zen here under the priest Butchō, who lives nearby. Wikipedia says only that meditation seems not to have calmed his mind.
suggested_refs: The Bashō-an historic site and Bashō Memorial Museum, Tokiwa, Kōtō ward, Tokyo

stops.name: Fukagawa, the hut burns
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter of 1682; day unrecorded
stops.campa: Fire takes the Fukagawa hut in the Tenna blaze of that winter, one of the conflagrations Edo suffers so regularly its citizens have a word for them. He is left without a roof and shelters the season out away from the city. Disciples build him a second hut on the same ground the following winter, and a third a decade after that. The address in the poems stays the same through all three. The buildings do not. He is thirty-eight, and the school he has built around himself is two years old.
suggested_refs: The Edo fires of the Tenna era, which destroyed the first Bashō-an

stops.name: Iga, the mother's death
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: His mother dies in Iga and he travels home for the mourning. Disciples build him a second hut in Fukagawa that same winter, so that he returns from a grave to a house raised by students. What he does with the death is delay it: the verse the corpus remembers, a lock of the dead woman's white hair melting in his palm like autumn frost, belongs to the next year's journey, when he comes back to Ueno as a traveler rather than as a son. For 1683 there is a death in Iga and a walk back to Edo, and nothing written down in between.
suggested_refs: The Matsuo family grave at Ueno, visited again on the Nozarashi journey of 1684

segments.name: Nozarashi Kikō and the Short Journals

stops.name: Edo, setting out weather-exposed
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1684; month and day approximate
stops.campa: He leaves Edo on the first of four long journeys, west toward Mount Fuji, Ise, his own province, and Kyoto, and titles the record he will make of it Nozarashi Kikō, the account of a skeleton left out in the weather. The title is the wager: he writes as a man who expects to die on the road and be found bleached in a field. He is forty. Ibn Battuta had opened his own travel book three and a half centuries earlier with a vow never to walk the same road twice. Bashō opens his with a corpse.
suggested_refs: Nozarashi Kikō (Record of a Weather-Exposed Skeleton), published after his return in 1685

stops.name: Fujikawa, the child by the river
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1684 journey; month approximate, day unrecorded
stops.campa: On the Tōkaidō where it crosses the Fuji river he passes a small child abandoned by the water, crying, left by parents who could not feed it through the winter. He leaves a little food and walks on. The verse he sets down speaks of the cry of monkeys, and the prose under it asks whether heaven or a father did this, and answers neither. No witness confirms the encounter; the scene is his own report, shaped for the page. Scholars argue about how literally to read it and do not settle the argument.
suggested_refs: The Tōkaidō crossing of the Fuji river, near present-day Fuji City, Shizuoka
sources: ja.wikipedia, '富士川' (river mouth and crossing coordinate)

stops.name: Ise, turned back at the precinct
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1684 journey; month and day approximate
stops.campa: He comes to the Grand Shrine of Ise in the habit of a wandering monk and is not admitted past the outer precinct: the shrine bars Buddhist clergy from its inner ground, an exclusion older than his lifetime, and his costume of renunciation reads at this gate as the wrong religion. He worships from where he is allowed to stand. Two and a quarter centuries later Hermann Keyserling will pass through Ise and Nara studying temple gardens and conclude that Japan has no metaphysics because it needs none.
suggested_refs: The Naikū (Inner Shrine) of Ise Jingū and its exclusion rules against Buddhist clergy

stops.name: Yoshino, looking for Saigyō's hermitage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1684-1685 journey; month approximate
stops.campa: He climbs into the cherry hills of Yoshino, ground made sacred by poetry rather than by rite: the wandering monk Saigyō walked here five centuries before him and wrote it, and Bashō treats Saigyō all his life as the model for how a man may walk and write at once. Half in earnest he searches the trees for traces of the hermitage. He does not find it. Four years on he will walk north to Matsushima and Hiraizumi after the same thing, another poet's ground rather than a god's house.
suggested_refs: The cherry hillsides of Yoshino, Nara Prefecture, and the traditional site of Saigyō's hut

stops.name: Fukagawa, the old pond
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day traditional
stops.campa: At the hut he writes the seventeen syllables that will carry his name further than the rest of the corpus combined: an ancient pond, a frog jumps in, the sound of water. Edo's poets hold a frog-themed linked-verse contest that year and his hokku places first. The verse reports an event lasting about a second. Zen, silence, the instant of awakening: every reading laid over it since is a reading. The poem itself states a pond, an animal, and the sound of water.
stops.quote: Many of my followers can write hokku as well as I can. Where I show who I really am is in linking haikai verses.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bashō; quoted in Wikipedia, 'Matsuo Bashō' (underlying work and translator not named there)
suggested_refs: The 1686 Edo frog-themed haikai no renga contest, at which the hokku placed first

stops.name: Kashima, the moon that does not come
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1687; month and day approximate
stops.campa: He travels east with Sora and the monk Sōha to view the harvest moon at Kashima, and to visit Butchō, his Zen teacher, who has retired to a temple nearby. Rain comes on the appointed night and there is no moon. The short journal he makes of it, Kashima Kikō, says so plainly instead of inventing better weather. It is a rehearsal for the road books to come: prose threaded with verse, and a plan the sky declines to honor. He is forty-three and has not yet walked north.
suggested_refs: Kashima Jingū and Konponji, where Butchō had retired
Kashima Kikō, conventionally the shortest of the travel journals

stops.name: Obasute, the moon over Granny Discard
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1688; coordinate unconfirmed, sources give the Obasute viewing ground only loosely
stops.campa: He detours into Shinano to see the moon over Obasute, Granny Discard, a hillside carrying the legend of an old woman left there by her family to die. The place name is loaded with grief before he arrives, which is why he goes. He travels with a servant and a horse, more comfortably than he likes to be seen traveling, and the journal is faintly apologetic about it. Sarashina Kikō is short, and it closes not at Obasute but on the wind coming off Mount Asama, blowing stones.
suggested_refs: The Obasute moon-viewing ground and Chōraku-ji, Chikuma City, Nagano
Zenkōji, visited on the same journey

segments.name: The Narrow Road: Out of Edo

stops.name: Senju, the parting at the ferry
stops.date_confidence: attested: 27th day, 3rd month, Genroku 2, converted to the Gregorian calendar
stops.campa: He boards a boat at Fukagawa with Kawai Sora and lands at Senju, the last ferry before Edo gives out into open road. Friends stand on the bank crying. He is forty-five, in poor health, bound for a northern interior that Edo poets read about and do not visit, and he opens the book he will make of it by invoking Li Po and Du Fu, wanderers who died out on the road. Ahead of him lie about a hundred and fifty-six days and some twenty-four hundred kilometers, mostly on foot.
stops.quote: The months and days are the travellers of eternity. The years that come and go are also voyagers.
stops.quote_source: Bashō, Oku no Hosomichi, opening line, trans. Donald Keene (as quoted on the Wikipedia article 'Oku no Hosomichi')
suggested_refs: The Senju ferry landing on the north bank of the Sumida
Sora zuikō nikki, Kawai Sora's day-by-day travel diary

stops.name: Sōka, the first night on the Nikkō road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the finished prose says Sōka, Sora's diary says Kasukabe; the discrepancy is not resolved
stops.campa: The finished prose puts the first night's lodging at Sōka, a post town on the Nikkō highway, and spends the passage not on the town but on the poet's own overloaded bag: a paper coat against cold, a nightgown, an inkstone, brushes, and parting gifts from well-wishers that he cannot bring himself to leave in a ditch though every ounce costs him. Sora's diary, kept day by day, puts the first night at Kasukabe instead. The two accounts of one journey will disagree like this for four months.
stops.quote: I patched my torn trousers and changed the cord on my bamboo hat.
stops.quote_source: Bashō, Oku no Hosomichi, trans. Donald Keene (as quoted on the Wikipedia article 'Oku no Hosomichi')
suggested_refs: The Sōka-juku post station on the Nikkō Kaidō
Sora zuikō nikki, which places the first night at Kasukabe

stops.name: Nikkō, the shrine of the Tokugawa
stops.date_confidence: attested: 1st day, 4th month, Genroku 2, converted to the Gregorian calendar
stops.campa: He reaches the mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu, the most lavishly gilded shrine complex in the country, and writes a hokku so deferential it reads as tribute: leaves of green, young leaves, and the light of the sun. Some readers take the reverence straight. Others notice that a traveler is about to disappear north into country the ruling clan barely administers, and that a man writes at a shrine to that clan what the shrine expects to hear. The text does not adjudicate between the two readings.
suggested_refs: Nikkō Tōshō-gū, mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu

stops.name: Kurobane, a fortnight with the falconers
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival on the 4th day of the 4th month, departure around the 16th, Genroku 2
stops.campa: He stops at Kurobane in the guest rooms of a samurai family connected to a haikai acquaintance and stays roughly a fortnight, an unusually long halt in a book whose subject is motion. He hunts with local falconers and walks in a temple garden. Sora's diary, which keeps the dates the finished prose does not, shows the days stretching longer here than Oku no Hosomichi lets on, one of several places where the two records of a single journey pull apart from each other.
suggested_refs: Kurobane Castle, now Ōtawara City, Tochigi
Sora zuikō nikki, source for the Kurobane dates

stops.name: Unganji, the teacher's five-foot hut
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Kurobane fortnight; exact day approximate
stops.campa: He climbs to Unganji to find the ruined hermitage of Butchō, his own Zen teacher, who was chief priest here before Fukagawa. The hut was five feet square, and Butchō had left a verse mocking not its solitude but its size, saying even that much was more room than he needed. Bashō copies the joke down with approval. Poem stones for both men stand on the temple ground now, re-erected in 1879: master and student set in stone at a hut that no longer exists.
suggested_refs: Unganji, Ōtawara City, Tochigi, and the poem stones for Butchō and Bashō re-erected in 1879

stops.name: Sesshō-seki, the killing stone
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 4th month, Genroku 2; exact day unrecorded
stops.campa: In the volcanic ground near Nasu he visits the Sesshō-seki, the killing stone, said to be the transformed body of a nine-tailed fox spirit and to breathe out poison on whatever comes near it. He finds bees and butterflies lying dead in the grass around it. He does not distinguish between the legend's venom and the sulfur the vents are actually emitting, and the journal grants the fox spirit exactly the weight it grants a battlefield or a shrine: a thing at a place, written down.
suggested_refs: The Sesshō-seki in the Nasu volcanic zone, near Nasu-Yumoto, Tochigi

stops.name: Shirakawa, the barrier
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 4th month, Genroku 2; exact day unrecorded
stops.campa: The barrier of Shirakawa marked, for four centuries of court poets who never went through it, the edge between the governed country and the north. By his day the checkpoint has fallen down and the threshold is entirely literary. He arrives conscious of every poem written about this exact crossing and admits he cannot find words equal to it. The admission of failure becomes one of the most quoted passages in the book. Past this line the place names in the text stop being ones his readers know.
stops.quote: When spring came and there was mist in the air, I thought of crossing the Barrier of Shirakawa into Oku.
stops.quote_source: Bashō, Oku no Hosomichi, trans. Donald Keene (as quoted on the Wikipedia article 'Oku no Hosomichi')
suggested_refs: The Shirakawa no Seki site at Hata-juku, Shirakawa City, Fukushima

stops.name: Iizuka, the fever night
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 4th month, Genroku 2; exact day approximate
stops.campa: He falls ill at Iizuka and spends the night in a farmhouse with a leaking roof, fleas, mosquitoes, thunder, and rain, an old chronic complaint flaring badly enough that he doubts he can go on. He writes the misery down without softening it. Sora, keeping his own diary a few feet away, spells the place Iizaka; Bashō spells it Iizuka, and both spellings survive in the record. The passage names the illness only as a long-standing complaint and never says what it was.
suggested_refs: Iizaka Onsen, Fukushima City, where Sora and Bashō spell the place name differently
sources: ja.wikipedia, '飯坂温泉' (coordinate and the spelling divergence)

stops.name: Kasajima, the grave not reached
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 5th month, Genroku 2; exact day unrecorded
stops.campa: He means to visit the grave of Fujiwara Sanekata, a Heian courtier-poet exiled north who died out here in 999 when his horse fell on him. Early summer rains have turned the road to mud and he cannot reach it. Someone points out the direction, and he looks that way and writes down that he looked. The verse asks where Kasajima is and answers with the mud of the fifth month. The book states the gap as a gap rather than filling it with a visit he did not make.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Fujiwara no Sanekata at Kitano, Natori City, Miyagi
sources: ja.wikipedia, '藤原実方' (tomb location and death)

stops.name: Sendai, the iris sandals
stops.date_confidence: attested: 4th and 5th days, 5th month, Genroku 2, converted to the Gregorian calendar
stops.campa: In Sendai a painter and amateur poet named Kaemon walks the pair through the bush-clover meadows of Miyagino and gives them straw sandals with cords dyed in iris, for luck on the road, along with a hand-drawn map of what is worth seeing further north. Bashō pays for it with a verse tying the iris cords of the sandals to the sweet-flag leaves people hang from their eaves at the summer festival. The pair go north from Sendai on Kaemon's drawings, toward places neither of them has seen.
suggested_refs: The Miyagino bush-clover meadows and Tsutsuji-ga-oka, Sendai

stops.name: Taga, the stone that survived
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 5th month, Genroku 2; exact day unrecorded
stops.campa: At the ruins of Taga Castle he finds the Tsubo no Ishibumi, an inscribed stone more than nine hundred years old recording the fort's founding and its repair. He is moved nearly to tears simply that it is still standing, when the walls it describes are gone and most of what the centuries touched has been rubbed out. He calls the encounter one of the journey's real joys and copies the inscription into his own prose. The stone is still standing at Tagajō; the fort it names is a field.
suggested_refs: The Tsubo no Ishibumi (Taga Castle stele), Tagajō, Miyagi

stops.name: Matsushima, the islands and the silence
stops.date_confidence: attested: 9th and 10th days, 5th month, Genroku 2, converted to the Gregorian calendar
stops.campa: The bay is scattered with hundreds of pine-covered islets and he has wanted to see it for years. He composes nothing. The prose says the view exceeds what words would add, and the published text carries no hokku of his own here; the line every Japanese reader knows, Matsushima ya, aa Matsushima ya, Matsushima ya, is credited in its earliest printing, the Matsushima Zushi of 1820, to a kyōka poet called Tawara-bō, while a separate tradition gives it to Sora. The most famous thing Bashō said here is a thing he did not say.
suggested_refs: Zuiganji temple, Matsushima
Matsushima Zushi (1820), earliest print attribution of the apocryphal verse

stops.name: Hiraizumi, the summer grasses
stops.date_confidence: attested: 13th day, 5th month, Genroku 2, converted to the Gregorian calendar
stops.campa: He stands where the northern Fujiwara built a capital to rival Kyoto and finds a field of summer grass over the mound where Yoshitsune made his last stand. Three generations of glory, an army, a treasury, and a war, and the ground has closed over all of it in five hundred years. He writes the line the whole country will keep. Then he climbs to the Golden Hall, sheathed in gold leaf and standing only because someone built an outer shed around it against the same weather that took everything else.
stops.quote: Ah, summer grasses! All that remains of the warriors' dreams.
stops.quote_source: Bashō, Oku no Hosomichi, at Hiraizumi; English rendering as quoted on the Wikipedia article 'Hiraizumi, Iwate' (translator not named there)
suggested_refs: Chūson-ji and the Konjikidō (Golden Hall), Hiraizumi, Iwate

segments.name: Dewa: The Mountains and the Sea of Japan

stops.name: Naruko, the Shitomae barrier
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 5th and 6th months, Genroku 2; exact day unrecorded
stops.campa: The road turns west and inland through the hot springs at Naruko toward the Shitomae barrier into Dewa. The guards here see so few travelers that they question the two men at length before letting them by. He waits out rain at a barrier keeper's house and writes the hokku about fleas, lice, and a horse pissing beside his pillow. A local guide then walks them over the worst of the mountain after dark, through country Bashō calls genuinely dangerous, and they come down into Dewa in the evening.
suggested_refs: The Shitomae no Seki barrier site, Naruko, Miyagi

stops.name: Ōbanazawa, the safflower merchant
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 6th month, Genroku 2; exact day approximate
stops.campa: He lodges at Ōbanazawa with Seifū, a wealthy safflower merchant who writes haikai and treats the pair as honored guests rather than as passing monks. The hokku Bashō leaves for his host makes the coolness of the house into his own dwelling. The other verse he writes here looks at the silkworm households of the district and says the people who tend them keep the appearance of antiquity. He stays several days, the longest halt since the fortnight at Kurobane. Sora's diary keeps the count.
suggested_refs: The Seifū residence at Ōbanazawa, Yamagata, and the safflower trade that paid for it

stops.name: Ryūshakuji, the cicadas in the rock
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 5th month, Genroku 2 in the text; Gregorian day approximate
stops.campa: On a friend's urging he goes miles out of his route to Ryūshakuji, a temple built into a cliff above Yamadera and reached by a long stone stair. Among the boulders and the old cryptomeria, in a silence that is not silent, he writes: stillness, and the cry of the cicadas soaking into the rock. The verse puts noise and quiet in the same instant at the same place and refuses to choose between them. It is the second of the two poems by which the country will remember him.
suggested_refs: Risshaku-ji (Yamadera), Yamagata, and its thousand-step stone stair

stops.name: Haguro, the three peaks of Dewa
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 6th month, Genroku 2; exact day unrecorded
stops.campa: He climbs Mount Haguro, first of the three sacred peaks of Dewa with Gassan and Yudono, and the head priest of the mountain's mixed Buddhist and Shinto order receives him and asks for a linked-verse sequence during the stay. He writes of moonlight and cloud gathering at the summit hall as though centuries of ascetic practice had settled physically into the timber. The three peaks together, he notes, are held too sacred to describe fully, and he stops describing them.
suggested_refs: The Dewa Sanzan: Haguro, Gassan, and Yudono, and their Shugendō order

stops.name: Kisakata, the lagoon that is no longer there
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 6th month, Genroku 2, converted to the Gregorian calendar
stops.campa: Kisakata is a shallow lagoon full of pine islets, compared in his day to Matsushima and read as its opposite: Matsushima laughs, he writes, Kisakata grieves. He draws the comparison himself, and this is the northernmost point of the journey. In 1804, a hundred and fifteen years later, an earthquake lifted the seabed and drained the lagoon into rice fields. Nothing at the site now resembles the water he describes. Kanmanji still stands above what used to be the shoreline.
suggested_refs: Kanmanji temple, Kisakata, Akita, and the 1804 Kisakata earthquake that drained the lagoon

stops.name: Izumozaki, the Milky Way over Sado
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the verse is traditionally placed here, but Sora's diary records rain and cloud on these nights and scholarship argues for later composition, perhaps at Naoetsu
stops.campa: From the Echigo coast he looks out at Sado across a rough sea, with the Milky Way lying over the water toward the island that for centuries received Japan's exiles: an emperor, the playwright Zeami. Tradition attaches the verse to these nights at Izumozaki. Sora's diary records rain and cloud on the fourth day of the seventh month, and a body of scholarship holds that the poem was finished later, perhaps at Naoetsu. The most cosmic line in the book may not have been written where the book puts it.
stops.quote: the rough sea / stretching out towards Sado / the Milky Way
stops.quote_source: Bashō, Oku no Hosomichi; English rendering as quoted on the Wikipedia article 'Matsuo Bashō' (translator not named there)
suggested_refs: Izumozaki, Niigata, facing Sado Island
Sora zuikō nikki, entry for the 4th day of the 7th month

stops.name: Kanazawa, the grave of Isshō
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 7th month, Genroku 2; exact day unrecorded
stops.campa: He arrives in Kanazawa to meet Isshō, a local poet who had written to him and hoped for exactly this, and learns that Isshō died the previous winter, still young. He goes to the grave instead. The verse he leaves there asks the gravemound itself to move, and offers it the autumn wind and the sound of his own crying. The city's haikai circle, which has lost the man it was building around, gathers around the visitor in his place. The two men had written to each other and never met once.
suggested_refs: The grave of the poet Isshō at Kanazawa

stops.name: Yamanaka, the parting from Sora
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 7th month, Genroku 2; exact day approximate
stops.campa: He rests at the hot springs of Yamanaka and rates their water second in Japan only to Arima's. Sora, ill for weeks and not improving, decides here that he cannot go on and leaves ahead of him for relatives in Ise. Four months of walking, one lodging after another, one diary written against another, and the companionship ends at a bathhouse. Bashō writes the parting as a body splitting, a goose separated from its flock, cloud dividing over a mountain. He goes on alone.
suggested_refs: Yamanaka Onsen, Ishikawa, where Sora left the journey

stops.name: Tsuruga, the sand of the Yugyō Shōnin
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 8th month, Genroku 2; exact day unrecorded
stops.campa: At Tsuruga the innkeeper tells him about the Yugyō Shōnin, itinerant patriarch of the Ji sect of Pure Land Buddhism, who once carried sand on his own back to fill the muddy approach to Kehi Shrine so that pilgrims could cross dry. A Buddhist ascetic hauling dirt for a Shinto god, and the moon said ever since to shine unusually white on that sand. The innkeeper's story goes into the prose and the sand goes into the verse, and the man who carried it is named in both.
suggested_refs: Kehi Jingū, Tsuruga, Fukui, and the sand-hauling tradition of the Yugyō Shōnin

stops.name: Ōgaki, the clam torn from its shell
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival on the 21st day, 8th month, Genroku 2, converted to the Gregorian calendar
stops.campa: He reaches Ōgaki, and disciples and old friends come in to meet him, Sora among them, recovered enough to travel; the text says they greet him as though he had come back from the dead, so little had they expected him to survive it. He does not settle. Sixteen days later he is in a boat again for Ise, and the last verse of the book is a clam being pulled from its shell in departing autumn. The book ends with him getting into a boat, not with him arriving.
suggested_refs: The Oku no Hosomichi Musubi no Chi memorial at Ōgaki, Gifu, the closing site of the journey

stops.name: Ise, the shrine rebuilt
stops.date_confidence: attested: departure from Ōgaki on the 6th day, 9th month, Genroku 2, converted to the Gregorian calendar
stops.campa: He leaves Ōgaki to worship at the rebuilding of the Grand Shrine, which falls this year on its twenty-year cycle: the halls taken down and raised again in new wood on the ground beside them, the god carried across, the old site left empty for two decades. Five years earlier this same shrine had turned him back at the outer fence. Oku no Hosomichi stops before he arrives. The book ends pointing at a building in the act of being replaced by an identical building.
suggested_refs: The Gekū (Outer Shrine) of Ise Jingū
The shikinen sengū of 1689, the rebuilding named in the closing lines
sources: Bashō, Oku no Hosomichi, closing lines

stops.name: Edo, the third hut and the long revision
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: He is back in Edo, having spent the years since Ōgaki reworking the prose and the verse of the northern journey, and settles into a third Fukagawa hut with his nephew Tōin and a woman named Jutei. The book will take him five years in all, out of a walk of a hundred and fifty-six days. Sora's diary, written on the spot, needed only the days themselves. The finished prose reorders the route and drops days the diary keeps. He is still working on it the year he dies.
stops.quote: Last year I spent wandering along the seacoast. In autumn I returned to my cottage on the river and swept away the cobwebs.
stops.quote_source: Bashō, Oku no Hosomichi, trans. Donald Keene (as quoted on the Wikipedia article 'Oku no Hosomichi')
suggested_refs: The third Bashō-an at Fukagawa, shared with Tōin and Jutei

stops.name: Edo, the gate shut for a month
stops.date_confidence: attested to the eighth month of 1693; day unrecorded
stops.campa: In the eighth month he closes his gate for about a month and refuses students, visitors, and gatherings. The withdrawal is associated with the last principle he develops, karumi, lightness: verse that stops reaching for weight and takes ordinary things at their ordinary size. He had built a school, a market position, and a reputation as the first poet in the country, and the final instruction he leaves his followers is to press less hard on everything.
stops.quote: disturbed by others, I have no peace of mind
stops.quote_source: Bashō, from a letter written to a friend late in life; quoted in Wikipedia, 'Matsuo Bashō' (recipient, date, and translator not named there)
suggested_refs: The doctrine of karumi as developed in Bashō's last years

stops.name: Osaka, the death at the merchant's house
stops.date_confidence: attested: 12th day, 10th month, Genroku 7, equal to 28 November 1694 in the Gregorian calendar
stops.campa: He leaves Edo for the last time in the summer, walks toward Ueno and Kyoto, and comes to Osaka to settle a quarrel among his disciples there. He falls ill with a stomach complaint at a merchant's house in Minami-Kyūtarōmachi and does not recover. Students gather at the bed. He dies at fifty, having told them he still had poems in mind that he had not written down. The road ends in a rented room, in a city he was passing through, over an argument between students.
stops.quote: falling sick on a journey, my dream goes wandering on a withered field
stops.quote_source: Bashō's deathbed verse, Osaka, 1694, accepted by his disciples as his farewell poem; as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Matsuo Bashō'
suggested_refs: The death site at Minami-Kyūtarōmachi, present-day Chūō-ku, Osaka
sources: ja.wikipedia, '松尾芭蕉' (date and death site)

stops.name: Ōtsu, buried beside Yoshinaka
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 10th month of Genroku 7, immediately after the death; exact day unrecorded
stops.campa: By his own instruction the body goes from Osaka to Gichū-ji on the shore of Lake Biwa and is buried beside Minamoto no Yoshinaka, the twelfth-century general he admired and had written about on earlier visits. The temple began as a hermitage raised by Yoshinaka's consort Tomoe Gozen to pray beside his grave. A disciple's verse marks the arrangement: the lord of Kiso and I, back to back in the cold. The poet chose to spend his afterlife lying against a soldier.
suggested_refs: Gichū-ji, Ōtsu, Shiga, and the paired graves of Bashō and Minamoto no Yoshinaka
Shimazaki Yūgen's verse 木曽殿と背中合せの寒さかな
sources: ja.wikipedia, '義仲寺' (coordinate, burial, and the disciple's verse)

stops.name: Iga, the Haiseiden
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: Oku no Hosomichi is printed in 1702, eight years after his death, and sells immediately. In 1793 Shinto authorities deify him. In 1942, three hundred years after his birth, his home province builds the Haiseiden, a memorial hall shaped like the poet himself, its round roof named the traveler's umbrella. Verse stones stand at points along the northern route. The man who wrote that the months and days are travellers of eternity is now a building, in his birthplace, wearing a hat.
stops.quote: The Narrow Road to the Deep North is Basho's study in eternity, and in so far as he has succeeded in this attempt, it is also a monument he has set up against the flow of time.
stops.quote_source: Nobuyuki Yuasa, translator's assessment, as quoted on the Wikipedia article 'Oku no Hosomichi' (likely from his 1966 Penguin introduction; not confirmed against the book)
suggested_refs: The Haiseiden memorial hall, Iga, Mie, built 1942
The kuhi verse stones along the Oku no Hosomichi route
